content:
According to Mark Gurman's latest *Power On* column, Apple is reportedly considering a complete overhaul of the App Store to boost the platform's potential revenue.

Apple's specific plans for the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and create more recurring revenue," a direction primarily driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

This overhaul is reportedly one of the reasons veteran employee Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020 and transitioned to the role of Apple Fellow, with responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller is said to oppose the idea:

Apple has various ways to improve App Store profit margins. For example, the company could eliminate the manual app review process—a costly procedure that has become far less effective in the age of agentic coding. However, users may not welcome further automation of reviews, even if doing so helps reduce costs.

Apple could also raise developers' annual fees, which currently stand at US$99 per year. Given that many small developers already spend US$200 a month on subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, some might argue Apple still has room to raise prices and developers would still pay. Apple could also charge large developers monthly fees based on usage, passing on some infrastructure costs to them.

The final outcome remains unknown, but I'm really looking forward to seeing what form these changes ultimately take.
